item.title: Introduction: Why AI Changes Investment Analysis
item.description: Have you ever looked at a stock and thought, “this could be a great investment” — and then gotten stuck? Too many financial reports, too many competing opinions, no clear place to start. That stuck feeling isn’t a personal failing. It’s a resourcing problem. Professional investment analysis — the kind hedge funds and wealth managers do every day — has always required a team of analysts working for hours, sometimes days, on a single idea.

item.title: How Investment Firms Actually Work
item.description: The firm and characters below are fictitious — a teaching case designed to show how professional investors actually work. The process is real.

item.title: The AI-Assisted Investment Workflow, Step by Step
item.description: Professional firms rarely deviate from a set process — not because creativity doesn’t matter, but because a repeatable process is what separates a good decision that happens to lose money from a bad decision that happens to make it. This article lays out the complete five-step framework this series follows, walks through how one idea flows from step to step, and shows exactly where AI does the heavy lifting versus where you have to.

item.title: Step 1 — Screening & Idea Generation
item.description: Screening is the process of filtering the investment universe to identify opportunities worth deeper investigation. With 4,000+ stocks on US exchanges alone, you can’t analyze everything — you need a filter, and the professional approach is to start broad and narrow systematically.

item.title: Step 2 — Fundamental Analysis
item.description: Fundamental analysis evaluates a company’s intrinsic value by examining its business model, financial health, competitive position, and growth prospects. The core question it answers: is this a good business at a reasonable price?

item.title: Step 3 — Technical & Sentiment Check
item.description: Fundamental analysis answers “what is the business worth?” Technical and sentiment analysis answers a different question: “what is the market willing to pay right now, and is momentum with you or against you?” You can be right about the fundamentals and still lose money if you buy at the wrong moment — a great company in a downtrend, breaking support, with negative sentiment, can put a fundamentally sound investor through a painful drawdown before being proven right.

item.title: Step 4 — The Bull/Bear Debate
item.description: Once you’ve formed an opinion about a stock, your brain starts working against you. Confirmation bias means you notice the news that supports your view and skim past the news that doesn’t. Anchoring means once you’ve decided a price is fair, you rationalize why it’s still fair even as conditions change. Overconfidence means you assume your analysis was thorough — which is rarely actually true.

item.title: Step 5 — Decision & Risk Management
item.description: Most investors can analyze reasonably well and still struggle at exactly this step: “I’ve done all this work — now what?” A simple buy/sell/hold rating is incomplete. item.title: Putting It All Together
item.description: Across this series you’ve moved from not knowing where to start, to having a complete, repeatable framework: a library of AI prompts for every stage of analysis, a full worked example, a decision-making process with real risk management, and reusable templates. Here’s the full workflow in one place, followed by the mistakes that undo it and a concrete plan for putting it into practice.
